content: Fraxinus is a genus of flowering plants that belongs to the family Oleaceae, which also includes olives and lilacs. This genus comprises between 45 and 65 species, most of which are medium to large deciduous trees, although a few subtropical species are evergreen. The common English name for these trees, ash, originates from the Old English word æsc, while the genus name Fraxinus is derived from Latin. Interestingly, in both Old English and Latin, the word also meant spear. The leaves of ash trees are typically arranged opposite each other on the stem, though occasionally they may appear in whorls of three. Most species have pinnately compound leaves, although a few species have simple leaves. The seeds of ash trees, commonly referred to as keys or helicopter seeds, are a type of fruit known as a samara. It is worth noting that rowans or mountain ashes, despite their similar appearance, are not true ash trees and belong to the genus Sorbus. Selected Species of Fraxinus Some notable species of ash trees include: Fraxinus americana (White Ash or Autumn Purple Ash) Fraxinus caroliniana (Carolina Ash) Fraxinus nigra (Black Ash) Fraxinus pennsylvanica (Green Ash) Fraxinus quadrangulata (Blue Ash) Fraxinus excelsior (European Ash) Fraxinus ornus (Manna Ash or Flowering Ash) Fraxinus chinensis (Chinese Ash or Korean Ash) Fraxinus mandshurica (Manchurian Ash) Fraxinus japonica (Japanese Ash) Ecology Ash trees serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, which include butterflies and moths. Threats The emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis), a wood-boring beetle native to eastern Asia, was accidentally introduced to North America in the late 1980s to early 1990s through solid wood packing materials. This invasive pest has caused the death of tens of millions of ash trees across 15 U.S. states and parts of Ontario, Canada. It poses a significant threat to the approximately 7 billion ash trees in North America. Research is ongoing to explore the use of three native Asian wasp species, which are natural predators of the emerald ash borer, as a potential biological control method. Public awareness campaigns emphasize the importance of not transporting unfinished wood products, such as firewood, to help slow the spread of this destructive insect. Uses Ash wood is classified as hardwood and is known for its hardness, density, toughness, and elasticity. It is widely used in the production of items requiring high strength and resilience, such as bows, tool handles, baseball bats, and hurleys. Ash wood is also a popular material for electric guitar bodies, valued for its bright, cutting tone and sustain. Less commonly, it is used for acoustic guitar bodies and drum shells. Additionally, ash wood is frequently employed in interior joinery and office furniture, often in the form of veneers. Despite its many uses, ash wood is not commonly used outdoors due to the low durability of its heartwood when in contact with the ground, which typically decays within five years. However, it is favored by woodworkers for its excellent finishing qualities, ease of machining, and compatibility with nails, screws, and glue. Historically, ash wood was used in the structural components of early car bodies and aircraft. The Morgan Motor Company in the UK still manufactures sports cars with ash wood frames. Ash wood also makes excellent firewood and is used for barbecuing and smoking. The two most economically significant ash species for wood production are White Ash (Fraxinus americana) in eastern North America and European Ash (Fraxinus excelsior) in Europe. Green Ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica) is commonly planted as a street tree in the United States. The inner bark of Blue Ash (Fraxinus quadrangulata) has been used as a source of blue dye. Cultural Aspects In Greek mythology, the Meliae were nymphs associated with ash trees, possibly the Manna Ash (Fraxinus ornus). In Norse mythology, the World Tree Yggdrasil is often depicted as an ash tree, and the first man, Ask, was said to have been formed from an ash tree. In European folklore, ash leaves were believed to repel snakes, and ash branches were used to draw protective circles. Irish folklore suggested that shadows cast by ash trees could harm crops, while in Cheshire, ash was thought to cure warts or rickets. In Sussex, ash and elm trees were nicknamed Widow Makers due to their tendency to drop large branches without warning.
